title: ‘Lucky Lu’ Leads Winners at MIFFest’s Malaysia Golden Global Awards
description: Lloyd Lee Choi’s “Lucky Lu” claimed best film at the Malaysia Golden Global Awards, presented during the closing ceremony of the 9th Malaysia Intern
body:
Lloyd Lee Choi’s “Lucky Lu” claimed best film at the Malaysia Golden Global Awards, presented during the closing ceremony of the 9th Malaysia International Film Festival (MIFFest) on Saturday.

	The U.S.-Canada co-production took the awards’ top honor, while the jury recognized filmmakers from across Asia, Europe, the Middle East and the Americas in a ceremony that highlighted MIFFest’s increasingly international competition.


	Egyptian filmmaker Morad Mostafa won best director for “Aisha Can’t Fly Away,” a multinational co-production spanning Egypt, France, Germany, Tunisia, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Sudan.
	

	Chilean-Argentine-Italian drama “The Red Hangar” emerged as one of the evening’s biggest winners, taking both best screenplay for Luis Emilio Guzmán and best cinematography for Diego Peguero. Accepting the cinematography prize, Peguero said: “This movie starts with a group of friends. I’m very proud that we turned our passion into such a great film.”

	Sri Lankan drama “Riverstone” also collected two acting awards, with Mahendra Perera winning best actor and Priyantha Sirikumara taking best supporting actor. 

	Taiwan picked up one of the night’s acting honors as Audrey Lin won best supporting actress for “Girl.”

	The best actress award was shared by Ong Xuan Jing for Singapore’s “Ah Girl” and Lila Gueneau for “Silent Rebellion.” “Ah Girl” also received the New Hope Award, recognizing director Ang Geck Geck Priscilla.

	The Audience Choice Award went to Spanish-French production “Sirât,” directed by Oliver Laxe.

	The ceremony also honored Chinese actor, filmmaker and producer Wu Jing with the Excellent Achievement Award. Wu attended the festival for a special screening of “Blades of the Guardians: Wind Rises in the Desert,” directed by Yuen Woo-ping. Accepting the honor, Wu thanked his collaborators and family, reserving his biggest thanks for his wife, whom he credited for her unwavering support throughout his career.
	

	Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong received the Lifetime Achievement Award. Lee said on stage: “I would like to accept this award not as a recognition, but as encouragement to keep making movies in the future.”

	This year’s awards reflected MIFFest’s growing international reach, with winners representing North America, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia. Southeast Asian cinema also maintained a strong presence through honors for filmmakers from Singapore, Sri Lanka and Taiwan.

	FULL WINNERS LIST

	Best Film: “Lucky Lu” (Dir. Lloyd Lee Choi)Best Director: Morad Mostafa, “Aisha Can’t Fly Away”Best Actress: Ong Xuan Jing, “Ah Girl” (tie); Lila Gueneau, “Silent Rebellion” (tie)Best Actor: Mahendra Perera, “Riverstone”Best Supporting Actress: Audrey Lin, “Girl”Best Supporting Actor: Priyantha Sirikumara, “Riverstone”Best Screenplay: Luis Emilio Guzmán, “The Red Hangar”Best Cinematography: Diego Peguero, “The Red Hangar”New Hope Award: “Ah Girl” (Dir. Ang Geck Geck Priscilla)Audience Choice Award: “Sirât” (Dir. Oliver Laxe)Excellent Achievement Award: Wu JingLifetime Achievement Award: Lee Chang-dong

title: ‘Incinerator’ Review: Award-Winning Japanese Portrait of a Teenage Loner Is Gentle to a Fault
description: Observing a seemingly ordinary world through the lens of teenhood can be a goldmine for filmmakers. From the perspective of young people who often f
body:
Observing a seemingly ordinary world through the lens of teenhood can be a goldmine for filmmakers. From the perspective of young people who often feel awkward and out of place, common dynamics can look strange, while unexpected connections seem like the most natural thing in the world. Shuntaro Uchida’s “Incinerator”, which won the Jury Prize in the Proxima competition at this year’s Karlovy Vary Film Festival, is of most interest for its peculiar lead protagonist, ten-year-old Kozue (played by a young actress credited simply as Karin). In her peaceful neighborhood outside Tokyo, this loner spends more time observing her surroundings than acting upon them, save for her habit of regularly stealing random objects to throw into the school incinerator. But while Kozue is a genuine, unapologetic weirdo, the film that is constructed around her soon betrays a less imaginative, more normative impulse — so much so that this coming-of-age story ultimately leaves a bitter taste.
	

	“Incinerator” wears its arthouse credentials lightly. Despite the film’s slow-cinema touches, its storytelling structure and emotionality — even though muted and quiet — recall instead the melodrama at its most facile. The characterization of Kozue’s parents feels especially slim, their clichéd attributes easy shortcuts to emotion. The mother is overworked, caring for the entire household but also for Kozue’s ailing and critical grandmother, while the father is an affable deadbeat; despite the film’s attempts to humanize them, they feel more like signifiers for “mom and dad” than actual characters. 
	

	In the middle of this familiar matrix, Kozue’s offbeat behavior stands out, creating initially intriguing situations and contrasts. As her mother gets home from work, for example, she once finds Kozue lying face down on the floor for no particular reason. The child isn’t loquacious, and neither is she interested in being understood, which would seem to open up the film to more original avenues than traditionally found in coming-of-agers. But the parents’ main reaction to their child’s eccentricity does not extend far beyond bemusement, and likewise the filmmakers can find little more to do with the character than wonder at how different she is. 

	Long, uneventful sequences capturing Kozue’s idle days spent daydreaming in nature or by the incinerator soon come to feel purposeless. If their goal is to grant access to her particular perspective, then that perspective seems only that of a bored and aloof tween. Kozue spends much of her time simply looking around, and there is pleasure to be had in the film’s soothing color palette and soft cinematography. But the promise of something more meaningful from these sequences is never fulfilled. 

	The issue might run deeper than the script, however: Even once something significant does happen to the young girl, the incident barely seems to register in the film’s emotional landscape. One day, Kozue locks eyes with Jinta, a young man who is visiting the school to perform a shadow-puppet show. Jinta is played by Taiki Shinozuka, heartthrob member of the Japanese boyband Timelesz; Kozue, however, seems interested in him not for his looks but for the way he moves through the world. He appears to operate on a different wavelength from everybody else — everybody, except for Kozue. 

	But neither Kozue nor Jinta seem in any way changed by their meeting. When she asks him to take her for a ride to a small village she remembers from childhood, the two then spend some time walking around the idyllic countryside, before returning home: This was not the place Kozue remembered, after all. What to derive from this sequence beyond a series of banal aphorisms about time passing and memories fading? Or from the deadpan goodbye Kozue and Jinta exchange after this trip: that sometimes we cross paths with people, and it feels like it might be meaningful, but it isn’t — except that it also sort of is? 
	

	Japanese author Kaori Ekuni, whose short story the film is based on, is often described as the “female Murakami”, and like adaptations of that other author’s work, “Incinerator” seeks to pause on moments both strange and ordinary, and let them unfold in whatever way they might. But nothing special happens, and no surprising meanings or emotions arise here. From its promising introduction of a strange little girl, “Incinerator” then trades in ordinary observations and emotions, as though afraid to force a point in any particular direction. What remains are cinematic aphorisms that may well be true, but cannot alone tell a compelling story.

schema.headline: ‘Incinerator’ Review: Award-Winning Japanese Portrait of a Teenage Loner Is Gentle to a Fault

title: ‘Haunting Adeline’ Adult Graphic Novels in the Works Based on H.D. Carlton’s Divisive Dark Romance Amid Film Adaptation Backlash (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A graphic novel adaptation of author H.D. Carlton‘s bestselling dark romance book “Haunting Adeline” is set to be released next year, Variety has le
body:
A graphic novel adaptation of author H.D. Carlton‘s bestselling dark romance book “Haunting Adeline” is set to be released next year, Variety has learned.

	Developed and published by Deviant Ink Publishing, a romance and dark romance-focused illustrated formats publisher, the project will first release as a comic book series scheduled to launch in early 2027 in comic book stores nationwide, followed by collected graphic novel editions for the broader bookstore market. Blackstone Publishing, which is currently in attendance at San Diego Comic-Con amid the announcement, will distribute the comic book series and collected graphic novel editions.
	

	“’Haunting Adeline’ coming to San Diego Comic-Con is something I never even conceived of, yet it feels so right, like Zade and Addie are entering into another home,” Carlton said in a statement to Variety. “I’m thrilled for my readers to immerse themselves into this world in a whole new way. I’d say I’m excited to see them lose their minds over it, but I think we all know they’ve already lost them long ago, and now it’s time to see their unhinged selves flourish at Comic-Con.”


	Per Amazon’s synopsis for Carlton’s bestselling, self-published book “Haunting Adeline”: 

	“For Adeline Reilly, moving back to Seattle was supposed to be the perfect fresh start. With her flourishing career as an author, and the inheritance of her late grandmother’s gothic mansion, there is nothing to stand in her way. But Adeline isn’t alone in Parson’s Manor. It isn’t the angry souls haunting the hallways of her childhood home that Adeline fears–it’s the mysterious break-ins, roses appearing, and threatening messages that somehow sound more like eerie promises. Adeline has a stalker. Yet, she quickly discovers she’s not the first person in her family to fall victim to a shadow in pursuit. Left behind are her great-grandmother’s haunting journals detailing the story of her own phantom, and subsequently, her brutal murder. Parson’s Manor now holds more than just Adeline’s memories—it houses a grim future that could lead to history repeating itself. If she doesn’t fall in love with her stalker first.”
	

	Deviant Ink and Blackstone say the upcoming “Haunting Adeline” comic book and graphic novel formats “will bring the world of Zade and Addie to life for the first time in an official sequential-art format, developed for adult readers, collectors, and longtime fans of the series.”

	News of the graphic novel project comes amid intense discourse in the BookTok community over Carlton’s July 14 announcement that a film adaptation of “Haunting Adeline” is currently in the works. At the center of the controversy is a debate between readers regarding adapting the book’s divisive stalker-romance storyline and explicit sexual abuse plot points for the screen.

	Carlton posted a new video message to Instagram Friday to “apologize” to those who “believe” in “Haunting Adeline’s” “right to exist as a book or a movie” who have been experiencing backlash for supporting the film adaptation, which Carlton says is still on track. 

	Variety has confirmed no additional details regarding the “Haunting Adeline” film are available at this time.

	Additional creative team announcements, cover reveals, retailer information and preorder details for the “Haunting Adeline” comic books and graphic novels will be released in the coming months.

	The graphic novel deal between Carlton, Deviant and Blackstone was arranged by Kimberly Whalen of The Whalen Agency.

	“Dark romance readers are some of the most passionate fans in publishing, and ‘Haunting Adeline’ is one of the titles that proved just how powerful that audience has become,” Deviant Ink Publishing publisher Eduardo Alpuente said. “This adaptation gives us the chance to honor the atmosphere, danger, and emotional intensity of H.D. Carlton’s novel while creating a visually striking new experience for fans. This is exactly the kind of project Deviant Ink was created to bring into the world.”

	“The fans got here before the industry did,” Blackstone Publishing CEO Josh Stanton added. “They were already making the art, sharing the edits, building the mood boards, collecting the merch, and turning ‘Haunting Adeline’ into a visual world. What interests us is not just the size of that readership, but the intensity of it. These fans do not engage with the story casually. That makes comics and graphic novels a smart next step, and working with Deviant Ink gives the project a creative partner built for atmosphere, character, and obsession.”

schema.headline: ‘Haunting Adeline’ Adult Graphic Novels in the Works Based on H.D. Carlton’s Divisive Dark Romance Amid Film Adaptation Backlash (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Sam Worthington, David Duchovny and Ke-Xi Wu’s ‘The Exiles’ Draws on Joseph Conrad’s ‘Heart of Darkness,’ Director Midi Z Reveals (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Taiwan-based Myanmar filmmaker Midi Z has revealed that his next feature, “The Exiles,” starring Sam Worthington, David Duchovny and Ke-Xi Wu, draws
body:
Taiwan-based Myanmar filmmaker Midi Z has revealed that his next feature, “The Exiles,” starring Sam Worthington, David Duchovny and Ke-Xi Wu, draws on Joseph Conrad’s classic novel “Heart of Darkness,” reimagined through a contemporary, original story.

	Speaking with Variety during the Malaysia International Film Festival (MIFFest), where he served as a jury member 15 years after his own directorial debut, Midi Z reflects on the unlikely path that led him into filmmaking, the lasting influence of Taiwanese auteur Hou Hsiao-hsien and how “The Exiles” continues a career-long exploration of identity and displacement.
	

	“I never went to film school,” Midi Z says. “I was simply someone who loved cinema. I learned from online reviews, books and whatever resources I could find.”


	One of the defining moments of his career came while he was studying in Taiwan. Selected for the inaugural Golden Horse Film Academy in 2009, Midi Z caught the attention of Hou Hsiao-hsien, who personally mentored him, selected his screenplay and even accompanied him on location scouts in New Taipei City for what would become his early films about Myanmar.

	The experience extended beyond filmmaking. After shooting, Hou would gather other filmmakers and actors, including French screen legend Isabelle Huppert, who had also been invited to the program for karaoke.

	“Hou told me, ‘You should go back and make films about your homeland,'” Midi Z recalls. That advice became the foundation of his filmmaking over the past decade and a half.

	“Southeast Asian cinema is different from Chinese-language cinema,” he says. “It exists on the margins, and it is deeply personal.”
	

	Inspired by Hou’s humanistic approach, Midi Z has continued making films across different countries while returning repeatedly to questions of migration, cultural identity and belonging.

	His newest feature, “The Exiles,” extends that thematic journey, inspired in part by a real criminal case in Southeast Asia.

	While Francis Ford Coppola famously adapted Conrad’s novel into “Apocalypse Now,” Midi Z says his interpretation moves in a different direction and tells an original fictional story.

	The U.S.-Taiwan co-production is filmed entirely in Taiwan, with roughly 90% of the dialogue in English. The film has entered early post-production, and Midi Z hopes to release it in 2027.

	“I see completely different aesthetics and perspectives across the 10 competition films,” he says of his role on this year’s MIFFest jury. “Every film has its own voice and its own identity.”

	As the number of film festivals across Asia continues to grow, Midi Z believes originality has become more important than ever. “Cinema is half art and half business,” he adds. “The biggest challenge isn’t learning how to make films. It’s how to remain original while trends and mainstream tastes constantly pull filmmakers in another direction.”

	Rather than chasing commercial formulas, he argues, filmmakers should embrace their individuality. “You don’t need to become mainstream,” he says. “You need to protect your own voice.”

	Looking ahead, Midi Z hopes to collaborate more closely with filmmakers across Southeast Asia, particularly in Malaysia and Thailand. Malaysia shares historical and cultural ties through a common British colonial legacy, while Thailand’s geographic proximity to Myanmar creates natural opportunities for cross-border storytelling.

	Having lived and worked across multiple countries throughout his career, Midi Z no longer defines home as a fixed place. “Everyone has to find a way to survive, both physically and spiritually,” he says. “The fluidity of identity and cultural belonging gives me the freedom to tell stories. It also gives me endless possibilities as a filmmaker.”

schema.headline: Sam Worthington, David Duchovny and Ke-Xi Wu’s ‘The Exiles’ Draws on Joseph Conrad’s ‘Heart of Darkness,’ Director Midi Z Reveals (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Josh Sapan on Life After AMC Networks and Championing Disability on Screen: ‘Neurodivergent Artists Just Bring Something Unique in How They See the World’
description: Josh Sapan, the former CEO of AMC Networks, left the entertainment company he had led through the peak TV era in 2021. He had helped transform the n
body:
Josh Sapan, the former CEO of AMC Networks, left the entertainment company he had led through the peak TV era in 2021. He had helped transform the network devoted to reruns of classic movies into a programming powerhouse responsible for some of the biggest shows of the aughts — a list that includes “Breaking Bad,” “The Walking Dead” and “Mad Men.” What, Sapan wondered, would be his followup?

	“I’ve always been interested in what you do after you do what you do,” Sapan says over Zoom. 
	

	The answer is a mixture of art and advocacy. For the past five years, Sapan has devoted much of his time to championing disability on screen through founding Marvels of Media Festival with the Museum of the Moving Image (MoMI), which celebrates the work of autistic media makers. On Saturday, Marvels will partner with the Academy Museum to present and program Disabilities, Representation, and Film Sensory Session. It brings together neurodivergent filmmakers, showcasing their short films, hosting a panel discussion and offering programming with sound and lighting adjustments in order to provide a more sensory-friendly experience.


	“The work is amazing and uplifting, and the filmmakers are really quite extraordinary,” Sapan says. “I have always been interested in people who see things a little differently. The greatest successes that I’ve been associated with are things that were probably considered unlikely, as opposed to likely. And neurodivergent artists, because of who they are, just bring something unique in how they see the world and how they tell a story.”  

	It’s a perspective that Sapan understands intimately, because his son, Nate, is on the spectrum. The goal of Marvels of Media isn’t just to highlight autistic filmmakers. It also offers them workshops and gives them a platform so they can get funding for their next projects.
	

	“I see it as a virtuous exercise,” Sapan says. 

	Since it launched, Marvels of Media has partnered with roughly ten theaters around the country, which serve as satellites for the program by showing movies and content from the media makers who are selected for the festival. 

	Sapan hasn’t given up on the media business. After leaving AMC, he launched Sapan Studios. In short order, it has backed several acclaimed indie films, including “Ghostlight,” “The Baltimorons” and “The Taste of Things” through a partnership with Independent Film Company, which is owned by AMC. That deal was recently extended and upcoming releases include “Mouse,” which is from the “Ghostlight” team of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson and earned raves when it debuted at the Berlin Film Festival. Sapan also has a television development deal with Warner Bros. 

	“It’s something that I wanted to do early on, but then I got on the executive track,” Sapan says. “This gets me a few steps closer to the actual artistic process.” 

	Now Sapan finds himself pitching projects instead of greenlighting them. That means having to navigate a business that is contracting because of mergers and consolidation. 

	“It’s not great that these legacy studios are going away,” he says. “But that disruption is not without its creative potential. It presents opportunities, too.”

	He’s also turned to writing, publishing “RX,” a collection of poetry in 2023, and “Third Act: Reinventing Your Next Chapter,” which profiles celebrities, government officials and business executives who have reached retirement age, checking in with everyone from Gloria Steinem to Rita Moreno and Alan Alda. 

	“We don’t always think of our lives as multi-chapter experiences, but they really are,” Sapan says. “When I was thinking of stepping down from AMC, the big question was what am I going to do? What’s my identity going to be? What you find out is it’s interesting to see what the world might invite you to do next or what you can make happen.”

schema.headline: Josh Sapan on Life After AMC Networks and Championing Disability on Screen: ‘Neurodivergent Artists Just Bring Something Unique in How They See the World’

title: Katy Perry Slams Trump Administration for Using Song ‘Firework’ in Military Strikes Video: ‘I Absolutely Do Not Condone It’
description: Katy Perry has blasted the White House for using her 2010 hit song “Firework” in a TikTok post depicting footage of military strikes. The video, pos
body:
Katy Perry has blasted the White House for using her 2010 hit song “Firework” in a TikTok post depicting footage of military strikes. The video, posted to the official White House TikTok account on Thursday, times the song’s lyrics — “boom, boom, boom” — to clips of bomb explosions with the caption “Iran has been warned.”

	“I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes,” Perry wrote in an X post on Saturday morning. “I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it.”
	

	“I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments,” she continued. “To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for. My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.”


I am deeply appalled and angry to see “Firework” used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes. I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it. I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and…— KATY PERRY (@katyperry) July 25, 2026


	The White House’s post comes as the Trump administration appears to be pausing a threatened major escalation against Iran while negotiations continue, although U.S. forces remain positioned for further attacks. Trump says Washington is “locked and loaded” but “not in a hurry,” claiming Tehran has become more serious about a possible agreement. At the same time, U.S. Central Command has continued striking Iranian missile, maritime and nuclear-related targets.

	Perry is one of many artists to fire back at the Trump administration for unauthorized use of their songs for political and often violent videos, in addition to campaign rallies. In June, Ariana Grande blasted the White House for using a version of her 2024 song “Bye” in a TikTok post that depicted ICE agents arresting and handcuffing people. Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, Celine Dion, Neil Young and the Rolling Stones have also criticized Trump for using their songs to rally support for causes with which they don’t agree.

schema.headline: Katy Perry Slams Trump Administration for Using Song ‘Firework’ in Military Strikes Video: ‘I Absolutely Do Not Condone It’

title: Wu Jing Honored at MIFFest, Says Hong Kong Action Cinema’s Influence Still Runs Through Every Wuxia Film Today
description:
Wu Jing says the fingerprints of Hong Kong action cinema are still on every wuxia film made today, including his own.

	Speaking with Variety at the
body:
Wu Jing says the fingerprints of Hong Kong action cinema are still on every wuxia film made today, including his own.

	Speaking with Variety at the Malaysia International Film Festival (MIFFest), where he received the festival’s Excellent Achievement in Film Award, the actor-producer reflected on Hong Kong cinema’s enduring influence while celebrating a special screening of “Blades of the Guardians: Wind Rises in the Desert.” 


	Directed by legendary Hong Kong action choreographer Yuen Woo-ping and adapted from Xu Xianzhe’s martial arts comic, the film was released during this year’s Lunar New Year holiday, grossing $215 million, and drew an enthusiastic response at the MIFFest screening.
	

	“There are more than 3,000 shots across exactly 125 minutes and 48 seconds,” Wu said during the post-screening Q&A. “I remember every minute of it, even every sound.”

	Asked whether he was satisfied with the finished film, Wu saied his feelings changed throughout the production process. “From the day we wrapped until the film was released, the score in my mind kept going up and down,” he says. “In the end, I give it no score, because once a film is released, it no longer belongs to me.”

	Having worked as an actor, director, producer and investor, Wu says wearing multiple hats is simply part of filmmaking rather than something extraordinary. “Every role on a film set is essential,” he tells Variety. “During breaks, we often put on someone else’s costume and try playing different roles. Everything you encounter  is valuable, and on a film set there are teachers everywhere you can learn from.”
	

	Wu says working across different roles has also made him a more humble actor. “It teaches you to respect every single person who helps create a character.”

	As technology evolves and short-form video increasingly dominates audiences’ attention, Wu says there is no definitive answer to how younger viewers will understand the wuxia genre.

	“‘Blades of the Guardians’ is made of our passion for wuxia,” he says. “Those of us who love wuxia told ourselves that even if the genre was disappearing, we wanted to create one last great martial arts spectacle.” Wu also points to the film’s unusually broad cast, whose ages span nearly a century.”We have a master who introduced both Jet Li and me to the industry, and he’s nearly 100 years old,” Wu says. “Our youngest actor was born in 2020. That century-long age span reflects the history of wuxia itself.”

	While visual effects can enhance martial arts on screen, Wu argues that authentic filmmaking still depends on performance. “Wuxia action can be enhanced with visual effects, but the real kung fu of filmmaking is expressing a character through your body and moving audiences with sincerity.”

	Having worked on productions in different countries, Wu says one observation stands out above all others: the enduring influence of Hong Kong action cinema.

	“Action choreography around the world traces its roots to Hong Kong.” he says. “Many action sequences today are built on techniques pioneered by Hong Kong cinema.”

	Wu identifies two lasting legacies that Hong Kong cinema has contributed to the global film industry: action choreography and production expertise. “In Hong Kong, a producer could oversee three films at the same time,” he says. “That was the beginning of filmmaking as an industrialized process.”

	Reflecting on the rise of short-form video and streaming platforms, Wu argues that technological change has always reshaped cinema without eliminating older art forms. “Cinema itself once replaced shadow puppetry. That didn’t mean Peking Opera or theater disappeared.” he notes. He believes the same will ultimately be true for cinema today.

	“Forms of entertainment will inevitably change,” Wu says. “Film, as an art form, will continue to thrive in new forms.”

schema.headline: Wu Jing Honored at MIFFest, Says Hong Kong Action Cinema’s Influence Still Runs Through Every Wuxia Film Today

title: ‘Bad Counselors’ Review: A Stealthily Christian Comedy Makes Believers of Two Rowdy Frat Bros
description: In a summer heavy on films we’ve seen before in some shape or form, “Bad Counselors” is nothing if not a novelty: a faith-based message movie masque
body:
In a summer heavy on films we’ve seen before in some shape or form, “Bad Counselors” is nothing if not a novelty: a faith-based message movie masquerading as a frat-bro farce, complete with PG-13 yocks and an “American Pie” alum cameo. Well, “masquerading” is perhaps unfair. Chris Dowling’s film is earnest in its attempt to extract specifically Christian life lessons from a familiar tale of manchildren forced into growing up, and goes pretty light on the Bible-bashing relative to others in its cinematic church. Still, it can’t help feeling like something of a zucchini-bread movie: more wholesome than it looks, in the manner of sweet treats devised by parents to smuggle vegetable content into their children, but ultimately less fun too.
	

	Following a limited theatrical run via Fathom Entertainment, “Bad Counselors” may find its widest audience on VOD — with an extended afterlife, perhaps, in youth church groups not unlike the one depicted in the film. Crossover potential is limited, unless the recent Prime series “Every Year After” makes a sufficient star of leading man Matt Cornett that his fans get curious.


	Cornett’s affable dudebro energy on screen goes some way toward balancing out the more obnoxious aspects of his character Grayson Fuller — a college-fraternity alpha jock introduced smoothly bluffing his way through a pantsless Zoom interview for a high-end finance internship. The interviewer is impressed, though he’d probably be less so if he saw Grayson callously hazing the frathouse’s beleaguered new pledge, or drunkenly heading out on the town with his best friend Tyler (Ramon Reed). The two of them party hard enough and often enough that local police officer Montgomery (Missi Pyle) knows them by name; when some particularly irresponsible carousing crosses a line, however, they’re slapped with a community service sentence.
	

	Good job that the night before, Grayson and Tyler accidentally stumbled into a megachurch worship session, mistaking the garish flashing lights and loud music for a regular nightclub — one of the better jokes that the film makes at its own side’s expense. There, zealous volunteer Becky (McKaley Miller) attempts to recruit the two non-believers as summer church camp counselors — an idea that, in the cold light of day, suddenly strikes Grayson as a good one. Movie law conveniently parlays their lengthy sentence into a week’s work at the cheery, picturesque Burning Bush Camp, where supervising pastor Tom (Chris Klein) sportingly overlooks their dubious childcare creds and eccentric prayer style. What can possibly go wrong?

	It’s a potentially funny setup for a culture-clash comedy of sorts. While Tyler finds himself warming to their new, sober environment, Grayson is mostly baffled by the rituals and regulations of organized Christianity — and isn’t very keen on kids either, least of all Patrick (Brayden Gleave), the eager, awkward misfit to whom he’s assigned as a mentor. 

	But “Bad Counselors” is at pains not to make Burning Bush look overly absurd, which, while fair enough, rather curbs its comic possibilities: There’s little irony or mischief in a film where every character is good at heart, and not much conflict either. What tension there is revolves around Grayson’s growing crush on goody-two-shoes counselor (and Tom’s daughter) Jenna (Brec Bassinger), which arouses both jealousy and suspicion in clean-cut youth pastor Dallas (Nathan Gamble, giving the film’s sharpest, most dimensional turn). 

	In any event, everything shakes out more or less happily for everyone concerned, with Grayson eventually resolving to forsake “the things that are trying to replace God in our lives.” There’s even some interpretive dance set to brooding Christian rock to nail home the point — by which point “Bad Counselors” has itself forsaken laughs entirely. If this all has you wistfully recalling the snark and satire of the elder-millennial Christian-youth portrait “Saved!,” it’s safe to say you’re not in the congregation for this film, and that’s fine. Still, it’s intriguing to see faith-based cinema taking new forms and approaches, and flirting, however briefly and gingerly, with danger.

schema.headline: ‘Bad Counselors’ Review: A Stealthily Christian Comedy Makes Believers of Two Rowdy Frat Bros

title: Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Holds Strong With $25 Million on Friday
description: With no major competition, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” extended its reign at the domestic box office as it entered its second weekend in theat
body:
With no major competition, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” extended its reign at the domestic box office as it entered its second weekend in theaters.

	“The Odyssey” added $25.9 million domestically on Friday, and by Sunday it’s expected to make $84.5 million. That figure represents just a 32% drop from its excellent $124 million debut. Through two weekends of release, “The Odyssey’s” North American total should land around $283 million.
	

	Over opening weekend, “The Odyssey” earned $264.1 million worldwide, an outstanding feat considering it’s an adult-skewing drama that clocks in at almost three hours. That godly haul was Nolan’s best global debut ever, legging out “The Dark Knight Rises,” which eared $249 million back in 2012. That film also happens to be the director’s highest-grossing film ever, at just over a $1 billion. At this pace, “The Odyssey” is gunning for that record as well.


	Second place went to the theatrical presentation of “Hadestown: The Musical.” The eight-time Tony winner pulled in an estimated $4 million on Friday. Rival projections have it earning $9 million through the weekend. Starring Reeve Carney, Eva Noblezada, Patrick Page, André De Shields and Amber Gray, “Hadestown” is a musical retelling of the Orpheus-Eurydice and Hades-Persephone myths. Crosswalk served as the distributor for the movie.

	Disney’s live-action “Moana” took third with just $3.1 million domestically on Friday. Through its third weekend, “Moana” is eyeing an estimated $10.8 million, which would push its domestic haul to $102 million. It’s a disappointing result considering the film carries a $250 million price tag, and it could end up costing Disney $100 million. Summer 2026 has been up-and-down for the Mouse House. While they’ve scored with “The Devil Wears Prada 2” ($688 million) and “Toy Story 5,” under-performers like “Moana” and “The Mandalorian and Grogu” ($340 million against a $165 million budget) have proved costly.
	

	“Toy Story 5” slotted at No. 4 with $2.9 million domestically on Friday. By Sunday, it should make $10.1 million, according to rival estimates. That would push the legacy sequel’s domestic total to a stellar $448.6 million through six weekends of release. “Toy Story 5” is expected to cross the $1 billion mark any day now and overtake “Toy Story 4” ($1.07 billion) as the franchise’s highest earner.

	Fifth place went to “Minions & Monsters,” which added $2.8 million domestically on Friday. Through its fourth weekend of release, the animated adventure should gross $9.5 million, pushing its North American gains to about $155 million. Despite being a relatively low earner compared to franchise favorites like 2015’s “Minions” ($1.15 billion worldwide) and 2022’s “Minions: The Rise of Gru” ($940 million worldwide), “Minions & Monsters” is holding strong, dropping just 30% from last week’s total. The film only cost $85 million, so it’s already a modest hit for Universal.

title: Pamela Anderson Shines in ‘Rosebush Pruning,’ the Year’s Most Twisted Movie: ‘I Like Stirring It Up’
description:
Last week, Pamela Anderson went viral — for her lush, enchanting garden.

	She’d never felt comfortable with the whole “sex symbol” thing after all,
body:
Last week, Pamela Anderson went viral — for her lush, enchanting garden.

	She’d never felt comfortable with the whole “sex symbol” thing after all, referring to that pleasure-seeking period as “the blurry years,” and is relishing this softer, quieter chapter of her life, replete with reading, tending to her 15,000-square-foot garden on Vancouver Island and plenty of soul-searching.


	“It’s a beautiful day,” she coos. “I’m on the island, loving my garden. It’s such a good place to unplug and refuel.”
	

	Anderson is experiencing a rare break since she’s never been more in demand. It all started with “Pamela, a Love Story,” an eye-opening Netflix documentary exploring her early life and years under the harsh spotlight. It was not only nominated for a pair of Emmys, but caught the eye of filmmaker Gia Coppola, who subsequently offered Anderson the role of a Vegas showgirl who’s aging out of the biz in “The Last Showgirl.” Anderson’s heartfelt, affecting performance earned her the best reviews of her career, as well as Golden Globe and SAG nominations for Best Actress. Then came last year’s studio comedy “The Naked Gun,” where she flexed her comedy muscles en route to even more critical acclaim, followed by a press tour where she and costar Liam Neeson earned plenty of ink cosplaying as a lovey-dovey couple.

	Now, the 59-year-old actress has four films coming out in the coming year, the first of which is “Rosebush Pruning.” Directed by Karim Aïnouz and written by Efthimis Filippou (who’s penned most of Yorgos Lanthimos’ films), it’s a provocative, pitch-black satire about a perversely affluent, incestuous family who believe that their mother (Anderson) was consumed by wolves. Tracy Letts plays her perverted husband, while Callum Turner, Jamie Bell, Lukas Gage and Riley Keough star as her very messed up children, and Elle Fanning is Bell’s paramour.
	

	“She was generous and open to taking risks. Her intelligence and sensibility, her refined sense of humor, made the character unique,” Aïnouz says of Anderson. “And moreover, she has a mystery and a charisma which is the trademark of a true movie star.”

	And when I say “incestuous,” I mean it. Everyone in this family is having sex with each other, epitomized by a scene midway through the film wherein Turner performs oral sex on Letts’ father while he furiously brushes his teeth. Anderson, 59, enjoys how “Rosebush Pruning” forces people out of their comfort zone and makes them confront the depravity of the filthy rich.

	“I like stirring it up and I don’t need to be liked,” she declares.

	Below, she tells Variety all about it:
	
		What attracted you to “Rosebush Pruning?” It’s a pretty provocative film, to say the least.	

	I thought it was timely and a very interesting script. I’m a fan of Efthimis’ and, of course, Yorgos’ work, and so between he and Karim, who I also love, I knew it was going to be visually stimulating and provocative. And I just felt like there is this epidemic of young wealth for no good reason. There is something to be said about that. 

	I loved when Tracy Letts spoke at the press conference and he said, “It’s about fascism.” It feels like a political film, in a way, but shown artistically, with Karim talking about patriarchy by using his visual and storytelling talent. So, yes, the film is disturbing, but so is a lot in the world. When I read the script, I thought, “This is really weird, but interesting, too.” I knew everyone wasn’t going to fall in love with it because art isn’t always popular. An artists’ responsibility is to confront the truth of things rather than chasing mass approval or trying to please everybody.



	

					Pamela Anderson in “Rosebush Pruning.”
									Mubi
	


	
		Could you talk more about this era we’re currently in where fascism is on the rise along with obscene wealth?	

	The fascism part is this narcissistic vapidness and empty style — a “clone me” AI unpoetic version of things. I felt this was an interesting expression of the times we’re in. It’s a shocking time and we can’t be too safe in our storytelling or be afraid to go too far. There’s nothing less interesting than inherited wealth, and there are generations of kids out there where I don’t know if they have a lot of empathy. I don’t like gore or gratuitousness, and I don’t think anything here was done for shock value. It’s all part of the story.
	
	
		When you talk about the flattening of culture and other aspects of society, do you feel social media has a lot to do with that? That it fosters an insidious type of groupthink?	

	I’ve always thought about that, even with my children. I’m always like, “What are your original thoughts? What is something you think that nobody else does?” It’s important to remember what we love and who we are, and I’ve found that in this chapter of my life I’ve done a lot of soul-searching, and some of it is through my work. Each movie is better than therapy. I don’t want [my kids] to get caught up in other people’s thoughts. It’s very important to remember, “I’m human,” and maybe we need to repeat that to ourselves. It’s a very fast-paced, wild time. And one thing I love about the movie is that it’s so unpredictable and you don’t know what’s coming around the corner. I feel like this is what the cool kids are going to watch.
	
		There is a moment in “Rosebush Pruning” where your character gets into a bathing suit and dives into her pool. Was that intended to be a nod to “Baywatch” at all?	

	No, not at all! I actually asked Karim if I could jump in the water and it was not in the script. I just felt like I needed to dive in. And I was playing older, in my 60s, and wanted to be free of worrying about what I look like and how I’m perceived. I am a mother, I am in my 60s and I am by my pool, so I told Karim, “Don’t shy away from this. I don’t care. The vanity is gone.”


	
		You were excellent in “The Last Showgirl” and received Golden Globe and SAG nominations for Best Actress. Were you a little disappointed that the Oscars overlooked it?	

	Oh my gosh! Well, that just seems wild to me to even hear you say something like that. I feel like I’m really at the beginning of my career, in a way. I’ve done a few films since “The Last Show Girl,” including this and “Place to Be,” where I play Ellen Burstyn’s daughter, and she’s one of my heroes. I’m taking everything in like a sponge and have so much more to give. I’m taking the rest of the year off to support the films that I’ve done, because I have four films coming out in the next little while and I want them to be seen. And then, hopefully, I’ll keep on growing, doing new things and challenging myself. But I was pleasantly surprised by how “The Last Showgirl” was received and how many people reached out to congratulate me on the film. Now, I feel like I’m in my groove.
	
	
		The last time we spoke, you were very critical of the Hulu series “Pam & Tommy,” and I’m curious if Seth Rogen ever reached out to apologize to you for that. I know you were seeking some sort of acknowledgement that this was an invasion of your privacy.	

	Well, it was. It was shocking at first, but I’ve let it go. It was a shock. And I feel like that was one of my hurdles as an actress: you want to have mystery to you. And I do have a lot of mystery to me, and there’s plenty that people don’t know about who I am, but when you have so much attention on those kinds of things, it really hinders your ability as an actor. So, I was disappointed. But when I got to play Roxie Hart in “Chicago” on Broadway, I used all that in my work. And then I was lucky enough to get “The Last Showgirl” and “Naked Gun,” and it’s kept going. My entire life I’ve used as material for my characters, so I’m not going to complain about it. It’s all good research.
	
		I enjoyed “The Naked Gun.” Are we going to get a sequel?	

	I don’t know. There have been a lot of changes at the studio [Paramount], so there are so many variables. Usually, when new people come into studios, new things happen. But I’m glad it did so well and I’m glad I got to do a big studio picture, and a comedy, and a scat solo! My upcoming part in “Place to Be” is not a big part, but there are no small parts, and whatever my part is, I want to give it the attention and love it deserves. I’m taking a break right now in my garden, which I like to do after every film. I just did a film, “Alma,” with Sally Potter and then went straight to my son’s wedding, so it took me a little time to regroup. After the wedding, I came home and now this is my decompressing time.
	
		How was your son Dylan’s wedding? That was in Saint-Tropez, right?	

	It was in Saint-Tropez, so it was absolutely gorgeous and beautiful and perfect, just like they are. It was wonderful to see Dylan and his beautiful bride there in a wildflower garden in Saint-Tropez. It can’t get any better than that. Saint-Tropez has always been a favorite place of mine. I used to get teased about it by my family, and now everyone seems to love it. So, there ya go!

	
		You’ve been tending to your garden for quite some time, but your gardening content has really blown up online of late. What does gardening do for you?	

	Oh, it’s very therapeutic. Right now, I’m surrounded by roses. I plant things all the time, and this year, everything just kicked in. As they say: sleep, creep, leap, and this is one of those years where everything is leaping out of the ground. I just take my clippers and my basket and go down to the garden in the morning when the sun’s coming up. I’m lucky enough to have a garden with an ocean view, which is unique and special. It’s really grounding, and I get a lot of my ideas and thoughts about characters there. I read in my garden, and sometimes, I even read to my flowers. 
	

	I know you live your life in chapters, and I know there were a few decades of wild-and-crazy — “the blurry years,” as I call them — but here I am, and I’m not taking this time for granted. This feels like a second chance that appeared out of nowhere. As soon as I thought, OK, I’m going to settle into my garden, make pickles and jams and write in my journal and I’ll be happy, all these films came up one after another.
	
		As far as turning the page goes, there were reports that you’d turned down a role in Fox’s upcoming “Baywatch” reboot.	

	I’d never heard anything about it! I didn’t talk to them about it. I think they spoke to my sons about producing or something, and they didn’t do it.
	
		You’ve long been a staunch advocate for environmental conservation and animal rights. How are you coping with a presidential administration that is the worst we’ve ever seen when it comes to those things?	

	We have to take those matters into our own hands and live as sustainably as we can. I love that my food comes from my garden, and I pickle and I’m as vegan as I can be — even though I don’t like that word because I don’t like to label anything. We should do the best we can and not push our views on other people as well; we should answer to ourselves. When I am home, I’m making these big soups and give a lot of my vegetables to the soup kitchens, family, friends and local schools.

	And yes, I am a pickler. I pickle cucumbers, radishes, anything. You can pickle anything! I did something with Flamingo Estate where we made pickles to raise money for animal charities, like the California Wildlife Center and Return to Freedom, who rescues wild horses. My friend Dan Mathews, who used to be the vice president of PETA, works for Save the Chimps, which is chimpanzees that are rescued from experimentation, so I did four big batches of pickles and raised money for these different charities that I’ve worked at and been to. If you’re on the pickle list, it means I love you! If you receive pickles in the mail, it always puts a smile on your face. You can’t be unhappy getting a jar of pickles. I’ll have to get your address.



	

					Pamela Anderson and Elena Anaya in “Rosebush Pruning.” 
									Mubi
	


	
		I love pickles. You once wrote an op-ed that I edited about freeing Julian Assange, and I know that was an important cause of yours. What is the status of your relationship?	

	There’s just a mutual respect and I’m glad he’s free and with family.
	
	
		On the “Naked Gun” press tour, when it was revealed that you and Liam had been romantic, what was your experience of everyone rooting for you guys as a couple? 	

	When there is chemistry on a film, that’s what you want — you want people to fall in love with the love that you’ve created onscreen, and that’s what people did. So, that was good! That means we did our jobs OK.
	
		You star in Michael Cera’s upcoming directorial debut, right?	

	“Love Is Not the Answer.” This is a complete transformation. My hair is red, and that was like a Hail Mary. That was an incredible experience with Michael. He brought things out of me that I didn’t know were in there. I’m very excited for people to see it. And then I did “Sundays” with Billy Bob Thornton, which is a more joyful character. The story is very sad, actually, but my character brings a little bit of light. And then I have “Alma” with Sally Potter. That was, like, a religious experience. It takes place over one night in London and it was wild. That’s a black-and-white film, and she’s editing it. And now, I’m just walking in circles in my garden. It’s been a crazy couple of years!
	
		You said that you feel like your career is just beginning, and given everything you’ve been through and all the ups and downs, how does it feel to now be considered a highly respected actress?	

	Well, I love that. I’m so grateful because I do work very hard; I study and work with acting teachers. I want to find out what I’m made of. I’m just scratching the surface and have a whole lot more to give. I want to ascend, and keep working, and be on the radar of all these incredible artists and talented people. I want to keep exploring myself. I feel like I have nothing to lose, so why not keep pushing?

title: Fox News Correpondent Peter Doocy Answers Trump's 'Transparent' Prez Question

body:
Fox News' Peter Doocy
                          If I Only Had a Mic!!!
                          Here's My 'Transparent' Answer for Trump
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 25, 2026
                            7:32 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  July 25, 2026
                                9:03 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            President Donald Trump sent some love to Fox News reporter Peter Doocy as he joked during his White House Correspondents' Dinner speech Friday night, but Peter didn't get the chance to answer a question the Prez asked him .... until now.
      
    
            Check it out ... TMZ D.C.'s Charlie Cotton caught up with the senior White House correspondent after the dinner and brought up Trump calling him out during his speech. Charlie pointed to the moment Trump asked PD who the "most transparent president ever" is.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            During the dinner, Peter asked Trump if he should stand up to answer the question, but the moment fell flat because Peter didn't have access to a microphone. No one would've heard his response.
      
    
            Well, TMZ DC to the rescue ... 'cause Charlie had a mic ready for Doocy's witty response -- and, while he didn't answer it squarely, Peter sarcastically harkened back to the moment a different prez called him "stupid," but with more colorful language.
      

        
                    
                  
      
    
            ICYMI, former President Joe Biden called Doocy a "stupid son of a bitch" during a White House press conference on January 24, 2022, after he had asked Biden about inflation impacting the midterm elections.
      
    
            Totally fair question, at the time, but POTUS clearly opted for insults instead of answers
      
    
            Peter's comments came after Friday night's smaller-scale redo of the White House Correspondents' Dinner took place at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, D.C.
      
    
            As you know, the OG dinner was rescheduled and placed under tighter security after a gunman fired shots back in April as the event was about to begin inside the Washington Hilton.
      
    
            It was the first time Trump attended the White House Correspondents' Dinner for during his presidency after previously skipping the event.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Last night's event went off without a hitch ... and Trump seemed to be in a great mood as he aimed jokes at CNN's Kaitlan Collins for her alleged lack of smiling, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, Bruce Springsteen, and several Democratic figures.
      
    
            He also joked about serving for a third term ... and even shrugged off an awkward moment when the Wall Street Journal was awarded for uncovering details about his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.

title: '90 Day Fiancé' Star Armando Niedermeier-Rubio's Daughter Rushed to ER Following Brain Bleed Hospitalization
description:
'90 Day Fiancé' Star Armando
                          Child Back in ER as Physical Symptoms Worsen ..
body:
'90 Day Fiancé' Star Armando
                          Child Back in ER as Physical Symptoms Worsen ...
                          Following Brain Bleed Hospitalization
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 25, 2026
                            5:46 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Armando Niedermeier-Rubio's daughter, Hannah, has been rushed to the hospital as she continues to grapple with the side effects from a scary brain bleed from an unknown source.
      
    
            Kenny Niedermeier shared the sad news on his Instagram Story late Friday night, telling fans their 13-year-old daughter was admitted to the emergency room earlier that day due to her physical symptoms getting worse.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She's undergoing more testing, and despite the health scare, Kenny said Hannah remains in "good spirits."
      
    
            As we reported, Hannah wound up in the emergency room in Mexico before being transported to the ICU in Phoenix, Arizona nearly two weeks ago for a brain bleed. TMZ obtained an exclusive photo of the three together.
      

            She underwent extensive testing during her week-long hospital stay, and they have been unable to determine the cause of her medical emergency.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She was discharged from the hospital earlier this week, and Kenny told TMZ Hannah was taking it easy and sleeping a lot as she recovered and prepared for more testing.
      
    
            While her physical condition had improved since her initial hospitalization -- during which she experienced weakness in half her body -- Kenny told us Thursday she was still suffering from partial blindness, weakness, and shaking, and was still on preventative anti-seizure medication and brain swelling medication.
      
    
            He also gave TMZ an update on Armando's temporary visa status -- we broke the news he was issued an emergency visa so he could be by Hannah's side after days of working with lawmakers to make it happen.
      
    
            But the visa expires Sunday, and Kenny says Armando must return to Mexico and then head back to Border Patrol to see if his visa extension has been granted ... and if not, he will stay in Mexico as Kenny cares for Hannah in Phoenix.

title: President Trump Experiences Awkward Jeffrey Epstein Moment During White House Correspondents' Dinner
description:
White House Correspondents' Dinner
                          Trump Smiles, Shrugs During Awkward
body:
White House Correspondents' Dinner
                          Trump Smiles, Shrugs During Awkward Epstein Moment
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 25, 2026
                            5:07 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            President Donald Trump couldn't duck these two words -- Jeffrey Epstein -- at Friday night's White House Correspondents' Dinner -- and it made for a seriously awkward moment.
      
    
            The moment came when CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer announced that The Wall Street Journal had won the 2026 Katharine Graham Award for Courage and Accountability for the newspaper's big scoop on Trump's past relationship with Epstein -- the late convicted pedophile financier.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Trump just smiled and shrugged his shoulders after Blitzer told the crowd the prez had filed a $20 billion lawsuit against The Journal, which included the home address of Khadeeja Safdar -- one of the reporters on the groundbreaking story.
      

            Blitzer also said Safdar's family was forced to relocate as a result of their address going public ... but Trump just brushed it off with a smile. Then, after Safdar accepted her award from Blitzer, Trump stood up and shook her hand, and some would call their interaction awkward -- just see it for yourself above.
      
    
            Standing at a podium, Blitzer introduced WSJ's investigation into Epstein and his relationship with Trump, as Trump looked on from his seat nearby in the packed ballroom of D.C.'s Waldorf Astoria hotel. Blitzer said the WSJ's reporting triggered the release of the Epstein files, thousands of pages of documents that might have otherwise been concealed from the public.
      
    
            As you know, Trump previously declared the Epstein Files are a hoax.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Wolf also said the Journal courageously published its story -- despite Trump's threat of a lawsuit -- along with a provocative letter to Epstein allegedly bearing Trump's signature.
      
    
            As WSJ reported, Epstein was given a photo album for his 50th birthday that contained the letter with a drawing of a naked woman and Trump's purported signature ... you can see it above.
      
    
            Trump just can't shake Epstein.
